note: Built by tools/course_rework.py from Kyenzo's own games; every position checked by Stockfish 16.

sacs.name: The Greek Gift (Bxh7+ / ...Bxh2+)
checklist: The bishop takes h7 (h2) with check and the king has to take or run.
A knight can jump to g5 (g4) with check, and nothing takes it for free.
The queen reaches h5 or the h-file in one move.
No defending knight on f6 (f3): an e5-pawn often chased it away first.
Check every king move: Kg8, Kg6 and Kh6 (and Kg1, Kg3, Kh3). You need an answer to each before you give the bishop.
A pawn on h6 or a bishop on e7 (or a queen that covers g5) shuts it down.

lessons.title: Attacking the Castled King: Mating Patterns and the Greek Gift
lessons.takeaway: Attack a castled king only with more attackers than he has defenders, and aim at the standard mating patterns.
rules: Attack a castled king only when you can bring more attackers than he has defenders, and use the standard mating patterns as your targets.
One piece rarely breaks a castled king, and three pieces often do. The patterns below tell you which squares to aim at and which defenders to remove first.

Colle-Koltanowski: The Colle is built for this plan. Bd3 aims at h7, Nf3 is ready to jump to g5, and with the pawn on e3 the queen reaches h5 along the d1–h5 diagonal once the knight leaves f3. The push e3–e4–e5 is the usual way to drive a knight away from f6, which is condition four. Check the exact move orders in the Colle-Koltanowski PGN and the Model Games Encyclopedia, because the final positions decide which conditions hold. Caro-Kann and Slav: Black defends the same geometry. A knight on f6 together with ...h6 or a bishop on e7 shuts the Greek Gift down, so learn to recognise when your opponent's structure allows it.

sacs.name: The f7 / f2 sacrifice
checklist: f7 (f2) is guarded only by the king at the start: it is the weakest square.
Bxf7+ or Nxf7 pulls the king out before it castles.
The follow-up must be ready: a knight check on g5 / e6, a queen check, a rook on the f-file.
Count what you win back: the rook on h8, the queen after a fork, or a mating attack.

lessons.title: Development Lead and the Uncastled King
lessons.takeaway: Ahead in development against a king still in the centre: open the position and attack at once.
rules: When you lead in development and his king is still in the centre, open the position at once and attack, instead of grabbing material or making slow moves.
Development is a form of time. Each piece you bring into play without him matching it is a tempo in hand, and tempi cash in fastest when lines are open and the king has not castled.

Colle-Koltanowski: The Colle develops fast and castles early, so you seldom face this plan. Your chance comes when Black delays castling to chase pawns: then e3–e4 opens the centre while the king is still there. Caro-Kann and Slav: Black's structure (c6, d5, e6) and early castling are designed to deny White this plan. If White grabs a pawn or sorties with the queen, answer with development and a central break.

sacs.name: The knight sacrifice (d5, f5, e6, ...)
checklist: The knight lands on a square their pawn covers. When the pawn takes, a file or a diagonal opens.
It works when your rooks and queen already aim at that line (the e-file, the long diagonal, their king).
Before you play it, see what you get back if they do NOT take: often the knight just stays there and wins.

lessons.title: The Initiative: Pawn Sacrifices for Time and Open Lines
lessons.takeaway: Sacrifice a pawn when the time and open lines are worth more, and when you can keep making threats longer than he needs to consolidate.
rules: Sacrifice a pawn when the time and open lines you gain are worth more than the pawn, and when you can keep making threats for longer than he needs to consolidate.

There are two kinds of pawn sacrifice. A dynamic sacrifice buys a short-term initiative: development, open lines and an attack. A positional sacrifice buys long-term compensation such as a bind or a structural edge (chapter 3B.3). This chapter is about the first kind.
The compensation audit. Score each line before you sacrifice.
1. Development lead: how many tempi do I gain?
2. Open lines: which files and diagonals point at his king or his weak points?
3. Piece activity: are his pieces passive or misplaced?
4. Structural damage: does the capture ruin his pawns?
5. The return: can I win the pawn back if the attack stalls?

sacs.name: The exchange sacrifice (a rook for a minor piece)
checklist: You give a rook for a knight or a bishop, and you get something that stays: their pawns broken, their best piece gone, a big knight, a passed pawn, or their king open.
It is positional: Stockfish says the position is still fine for you afterwards.
Typical: Rxc3 against the c3-knight, Rxf6 against the king's knight, Rxe6 to break the centre.

lessons.title: The Positional Exchange Sacrifice and Other Positional Sacrifices
lessons.takeaway: Give up material for lasting positional compensation only when the position cannot be opened against you.
rules: Give up material for lasting positional compensation (control of key squares, crippled structure, dominant minor pieces) when the position cannot be opened against you.

A positional sacrifice is accepted by the position, not by the opponent. The material is gone for good, so the compensation must be permanent. The classic form is the exchange sacrifice: a rook for a minor piece, often with a pawn. The same logic applies to a pawn for an outpost or a piece for pawns and a bind.
Types of compensation.
The compensation checklist. Check all six before you sacrifice.
1. Structural damage: is it permanent?
2. Piece dominance: will my pieces rule key squares for the rest of the game?
3. Rooks: can his rooks ever become active? Can mine?
4. King safety: whose king is safer after the sacrifice?

sacs.name: The rook sacrifice on the king's cover (Rxh7, Rxg7, ...)
checklist: The rook takes a pawn in front of their king to open it.
The other pieces must be ready to come in at once: a queen on the h-file, a bishop on the long diagonal.
Count the checks after the sacrifice: if they run out, the sacrifice was too early.

sacs.name: The bishop sacrifice next to the king (Bxg6, Bxg7, ...)
checklist: The bishop takes a pawn of the king's cover to open the files and diagonals around the king.
You need a second attacker ready to use the open lines: the queen, a rook lift, a knight.

lessons.takeaway: Attack a castled king only with more attackers than he has defenders, and aim at the standard mating patterns.

sacs.name: The queen sacrifice
checklist: Give the queen only for mate or for more material back: count the whole line.
Most queen sacrifices are about the back rank, a smothered mate, or a deadly pin.

lessons.title: Core Tactical Patterns
lessons.takeaway: Learn the six patterns until you see them before you calculate: fork, pin, skewer, discovered attack, back-rank mate, removing the defender.
rules: Learn six geometric patterns until you see them before you calculate: fork, pin, skewer, discovered attack, back-rank mate and removing the defender.
Tactics are not luck. Each pattern needs the same few ingredients on the board, and once you know them you can see the pattern coming from the position.
The six patterns. For each: what happens, the Alarm Trigger to look for, and a quick test.

sacs.name: The pawn sacrifice for time and open lines
checklist: A pawn for a lead in development, an open file against their king, or a strong square for your piece.
It works when they need moves to take it and then to cover the holes.
If you cannot name what you get for the pawn, do not give it.

plans.name: Queenless middlegame (queens traded by move 15)
steps: Queens are off: play it as an endgame. Bring the king to the centre.
Find the weak pawn on their side and put your pieces on it; make a passed pawn.

lessons.title: Middlegame-to-Endgame Transitions II: Conversion Technique
lessons.takeaway: Convert in three steps, stabilise, squeeze, strike, and keep asking what his last hope is.
rules: Convert a winning position in three steps (stabilise, squeeze, strike), and keep asking what his last hope is.
Winning a won position is a process, not a flourish. Most conversion failures come from relaxing, hurrying, or letting the opponent reach a perpetual check or a fortress.
The three steps.

Most repertoire positions begin equal, so conversion practice starts after a repertoire line has gone well and the opponent has made an error. Use the model games in the Encyclopedias to find those positions, and take the final stages of each game as conversion exercises.

plans.name: Half-open f-file for you (the f-pawn was exchanged)
steps: The half-open f-file: rook (or two) on f1, pressure on f7 (f2).
Combine it with the knight to g5 and the bishop on the a2-g8 diagonal.

lessons.title: Open Files and the Seventh Rank
lessons.takeaway: Rooks to the open files, double them, and invade the seventh rank.
rules: Put your rooks on open files, double them, and invade the seventh rank, where pawns and the enemy king are weakest.
An open file is a highway for rooks. The side that controls it decides where the rooks can enter the enemy position.

Slav and Semi-Slav: The Exchange Slav (cxd5 cxd5) leaves the c-file completely open, so the fight for the file starts early. Apply the triggers above to see who controls it and who gets the entry square first. Caro-Kann: In the Panov-Botvinnik with 5...e6, once the c-pawns are exchanged and Black recaptures on d5 with the knight, the c-file is open and White's d4 pawn is isolated. The rook fight for the c-file is part of the plan, and chapter 2.3 builds on it.

plans.name: Kings castled on opposite wings: pawn storms
steps: Kings on opposite wings: it is a race. Pawns forward against their king, fast.
Count the tempi: open a file against their king before they open one against yours.
Every move that does not attack or defend is lost.

lessons.title: Opposite-Side Castling: Pawn Storms and Tempo Counting
lessons.takeaway: With the kings on opposite wings, start the pawn storm at once, support it with pieces and count the tempi.
rules: When the kings stand on opposite wings, launch the pawn storm at once, support it with pieces, and win the race by counting tempi.

Opposite-side castling turns the game into a race. A pawn storm against his king costs you nothing in safety, because the pawns in front of your own king stay at home. The winner is the side that opens lines first and brings more attackers.

Caro-Kann: In the Classical Caro-Kann lines, White often castles queenside. Whether the kings end up on opposite wings depends on where Black castles, so check the PGN for the exact moves in each branch. When opposite-side castling arises, start the tempo count from the moment both kings have castled.

plans.name: Open centre (no d- or e-pawns left)
steps: Open centre: activity counts most. Rooks on the open d- and e-files, bishops on long diagonals.
The bishop pair is strong here. Do not trade a bishop for a knight without a reason.

lessons.title: Minor-Piece Imbalances: Good Knight vs Bad Bishop, the Bishop Pair
lessons.takeaway: Steer the structure toward the pieces that favour you: open it for bishops, close it and use outposts for knights, trade your bad bishop.
rules: Steer the pawn structure toward the minor pieces that favour you: open the position for bishops, close it and create outposts for knights, trade your bad bishop and keep the bishop pair when the position opens.
Key terms.

Caro-Kann and Slav: Black's pawns on c6, d5 and e6 all stand on light squares, so the light-squared bishop is the problem piece. That is why the repertoires develop it outside the chain early (chapter 0.3), and why trading it is acceptable. Colle-Koltanowski: White's pawns on c3, d4 and e3 all stand on dark squares, so the light-squared bishop on d3 is the good bishop. The dark-squared bishop on c1 is the one that needs a plan, and the e3–e4 break is the usual way to free it.

plans.name: They have the isolated queen's pawn
steps: They have the isolated pawn: block the square in front of it with a knight.
Trade pieces, especially the attackers (their knight on e4 / e5, their light bishop).
Then attack the pawn with rooks on the d-file. The endgame is good for you.

lessons.title: The Isolated Queen's Pawn (Both Sides)
lessons.takeaway: The side with the isolated pawn attacks while the pieces are on; the other side blockades the square in front of it and trades toward an endgame.
rules: The owner of the isolated queen's pawn (IQP) attacks while the pieces are still on the board; the opponent blockades the square in front of the pawn and trades pieces toward an endgame.
The structure. An IQP is a d-pawn with no c- or e-pawn of its own colour beside it: d4 for White or d5 for Black. A pawn on d4 guards c5 and e5, and the files beside it are open.
Strengths of the pawn. Space, control of c5 and e5, open files for the rooks, a knight outpost on e5, and attacking chances against the kingside, including the d4–d5 break.
Weaknesses of the pawn. It needs protection from pieces. The square in front of it (d5 for White's IQP) is a permanent outpost for the opponent's pieces. In an endgame the pawn is a target.

Caro-Kann: The Panov-Botvinnik with 5...e6 often leads to IQP positions: after the exchange on d5 and ...Nxd5, White's d4 pawn is isolated. In your repertoire you are on the blockading side. Put a knight on d5, trade pieces, and aim for an endgame in which the isolated pawn is weak. The structure is close to Semi-Slav and Queen's Gambit structures, which is why this line was chosen. Slav and Semi-Slav: You can meet IQP positions from the other side if a Semi-Slav line leaves a pawn isolated.

plans.name: You have the isolated queen's pawn
steps: You have the isolated pawn: play for activity and the attack, not for the endgame.
Knight to e5 (e4), a rook to the e- or d-file, the bishop on the b1-h7 diagonal aimed at the king.
Push d5 (d4) when your pieces are ready: it opens the position at the right moment.
Avoid trades: every trade makes the pawn weaker.

lessons.title: The Isolated Queen's Pawn (Both Sides)
lessons.takeaway: The side with the isolated pawn attacks while the pieces are on; the other side blockades the square in front of it and trades toward an endgame.
rules: The owner of the isolated queen's pawn (IQP) attacks while the pieces are still on the board; the opponent blockades the square in front of the pawn and trades pieces toward an endgame.

plans.name: You have hanging pawns (c + d)
steps: You have hanging pawns: keep them side by side and mobile.
Push one of them (d5 or c5) when it opens lines for your pieces; do not push without a reason.
Your pieces belong behind them, ready for the break.

lessons.title: Hanging Pawns
lessons.takeaway: Keep the pieces active and advance a hanging pawn only when it wins something concrete.
rules: The owner of hanging pawns keeps the pieces active and advances a pawn only when it wins something concrete; the opponent pressures the pawns and tries to force an advance at the wrong moment.

The structure. Hanging pawns are two adjacent pawns, usually on the c- and d-files, with no friendly pawn on the neighbouring b- and e-files: c4 and d4 for White, c5 and d5 for Black. Together they control four squares (for White: b5, c5, d5 and e5), and the b- and e-files beside them are half-open.
Strengths. Central space, mobility (either pawn may advance), control of key squares and open files for the rooks. The break d4–d5 or c4–c5 can open the game suddenly.

Weaknesses. No pawn defends them, so they need piece support. If one is blocked or attacked and must advance at the wrong moment, or if a trade leaves them without support, they fall. In an endgame they are often weak.
Hanging pawns are not a core structure of the three repertoires, but they appear through transpositions and in your opponents' choices, and players at 1200–1600 meet them often.

plans.name: Pawn chain d4-e5 against e6-d5 (Advance Caro / French)
steps: Pawn chain d4-e5 against e6-d5: attack the base of the chain.
With the chain: f4-f5 or a kingside attack (the e5-pawn takes f6 from their knight).
Against it: ...c5 and ...f6 hit d4 and e5; put pressure on d4 with ...Nc6, ...Qb6.

lessons.title: Pawn Chains: The Advance Structure and Attacking the Base
lessons.takeaway: Attack the base of the chain; defend your own chain at its base and play on the flank the chain points to.
rules: Attack the base of an enemy pawn chain, because when the base falls the whole chain falls; defend your own chain by supporting its base and by playing on the flank where the chain points.

The structure. A pawn chain is a diagonal line of pawns that protect each other, such as White's pawns on d4 and e5. The head is the front pawn (e5) and the base is the rearmost pawn (d4). The chain fixes its pawns on one colour of squares, so the bishop of that colour behind the chain is hemmed in. The chain also takes squares away from the opponent: White's pawn on e5 controls d6 and f6.

Where each side plays. A chain points toward the flank where its owner has space. White's d4–e5 chain points at the kingside, so White expands there, often with f2–f4. The opponent strikes at the base from the other side, with ...c5 and pieces aimed at d4.

Caro-Kann: The Advance Variation (1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5) gives White exactly this chain. The line chosen for the Black repertoire, 3...c5, attacks the base from move three. Whether White keeps the tension, takes on c5 or supports d4, the middlegame follows this chapter: keep pressing d4 with pieces and the c-pawn. If White releases the chain with dxc5, the structure opens and chapters 1.5 and 2.5 take over.

plans.name: They have hanging pawns (c + d)
steps: They have hanging pawns: attack them so that one has to advance, then block the square in front of it.
After the push, the other pawn and the square in front become targets.

lessons.title: Hanging Pawns
lessons.takeaway: Keep the pieces active and advance a hanging pawn only when it wins something concrete.
rules: The owner of hanging pawns keeps the pieces active and advances a pawn only when it wins something concrete; the opponent pressures the pawns and tries to force an advance at the wrong moment.

plans.name: Carlsbad structure (you have d4 against their d5 + c6, or the mirror)
steps: Carlsbad: the side with the queenside pawns plays the minority attack b4-b5 (...b5-b4) to give the other side a weak c-pawn.
The other side plays for the kingside or for the e4 (e5) break.
Knights love the square in front of the weak pawn.

lessons.title: The Carlsbad Structure and the Minority Attack
lessons.takeaway: In the Carlsbad structure White advances the minority attack (b4-b5) to create a weakness on c6, and Black counters in the centre or on the kingside.
rules: In the Carlsbad structure White advances the queenside minority (b4–b5) to create a weakness on c6, while Black counters with a central break or play on the kingside.

The structure. White has pawns on a2, b2, d4 and e3. Black has pawns on a7, b7, c6 and d5. White's c-pawn and Black's e-pawn have been exchanged. On the queenside White has two pawns against three, which is why the attack is called a minority attack. The c-file is half-open for White.

The idea. White pushes b2–b4–b5, supported by a2–a4 when needed, to exchange the pawn on c6. After bxc6 bxc6, Black has a weak pawn on c6 and an isolated pawn on a7, and White's rooks aim down the c-file.

The Carlsbad is the reference exchange structure for every Queen's Gambit family, so keep it in mind even when your repertoire route avoids it. Slav and Semi-Slav: It can arise when White exchanges on d5 and Black recaptures with the e-pawn. The Exchange Slav recaptures with the c-pawn instead, which leads to a symmetrical structure with an open c-file (chapter 1.4).

plans.name: Carlsbad with your queenside pawns: the minority attack
steps: Minority attack: push the b-pawn to b5 (...b4), trade on c6 (c3) and attack the backward c-pawn with rooks and pieces.
Before you push, put a rook on the b-file or the c-file and a knight ready for c5 / e5.

lessons.title: The Carlsbad Structure and the Minority Attack
lessons.takeaway: In the Carlsbad structure White advances the minority attack (b4-b5) to create a weakness on c6, and Black counters in the centre or on the kingside.
rules: In the Carlsbad structure White advances the queenside minority (b4–b5) to create a weakness on c6, while Black counters with a central break or play on the kingside.

The structure. White has pawns on a2, b2, d4 and e3. Black has pawns on a7, b7, c6 and d5. White's c-pawn and Black's e-pawn have been exchanged. On the queenside White has two pawns against three, which is why the attack is called a minority attack. The c-file is half-open for White.

plans.name: Doubled g-pawns after ...hxg6 / Bxg6 recaptures
steps: Doubled g-pawns: the h-file is open or opens. Rook to h1 (h8) and look for checks on the h-file.
The doubled pawns cover f5 and h5: use the other squares around the king.

lessons.title: Weak Squares, Outposts and Backward Pawns
lessons.takeaway: Find the squares and pawns he can no longer protect with pawns, put your pieces there, and guard your own weak spots the same way.
rules: Find the squares and pawns that he can no longer protect with pawns, bring your pieces to them, and guard your own weaknesses the same way.
Key terms.

Colle-Koltanowski: The square e5 is the natural outpost for a White knight, supported by the d4 pawn. Black's ...f6 would challenge it but weakens e6 and the light squares. Caro-Kann: In the Advance structure, White's pawn on e5 takes d6 and f6 away from Black's pieces, so Black should challenge the chain (chapter 2.7) before White's pieces settle on d6.

plans.name: Stonewall (d4-e3-f4 or d5-e6-f5)
steps: Stonewall: the knight goes to e5 (e4), backed by the f-pawn and the d-pawn.
Kingside attack: Rf3-h3, Qh5, g4-g5. The dark squares (e5 / e4) are the point.
Against it: trade the dark bishop of the Stonewall side, put a knight on e4 (e5).

lessons.title: Weak Squares, Outposts and Backward Pawns
lessons.takeaway: Find the squares and pawns he can no longer protect with pawns, put your pieces there, and guard your own weak spots the same way.
